title: Git & GitHub fundamentals
summary: Track changes to your code with Git and back it up, share it, and collaborate online using GitHub.
objectives: Explain what Git and GitHub are and how they differ
Initialise a repository and record snapshots with add and commit
Inspect history and status with log and status
Connect a local repo to GitHub and push your work
Use branches to work safely without breaking main
Ignore files you should never commit with a .gitignore

quiz.q: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
quiz.answer: Git is the version-control tool on your computer; GitHub is an online service that hosts Git repositories.
quiz.why: Git runs locally and tracks changes; GitHub stores a copy in the cloud for backup and collaboration. You can use Git without GitHub.

quiz.q: Which command records a snapshot of your staged changes?
quiz.why: git commit takes everything you have staged with git add and saves it as a permanent snapshot in the history, with a message.

options: Moves changes into the staging area
quiz.why: git add stages changes — it tells Git which edits you want included in your next commit. It does not upload or commit anything by itself.

quiz.answer: It lists files and folders that Git should not track, such as secrets, virtual environments, and large data files.
quiz.why: Keeping things like passwords, .env files, and venv out of your repo avoids leaking secrets and bloating the history.

quiz.q: Why use a branch instead of committing straight to main?
options: It lets you work on a change in isolation
quiz.why: A branch is a separate line of work, so you can experiment freely. If it works you merge it into main; if not, you discard it — main stays safe.

quiz.q: In what order do these three steps normally happen: commit, add, push?
quiz.why: You stage changes with add, snapshot them with commit, then send those commits to GitHub with push.

body_markdown:
## Why version control?

Imagine saving files as `report_final.py`, then `report_final_v2.py`, then `report_final_REALLY_final.py`. It quickly becomes chaos. **Version control** solves this: it records snapshots of your project over time so you can see what changed, when, and why — and roll back if you break something.

**Git** is the most popular version-control tool. It runs on your own computer. **GitHub** is a website that stores copies of your Git repositories online, so your work is backed up and you can share it with others or with your future employer.

## Your first repository

A **repository** (or *repo*) is a folder that Git is watching. You create one with `git init`. After that, Git tracks every change you choose to record.

```bash
git init
git add hello.py
git commit -m "Add hello.py"
```

There are three stages: your **working directory** (your files), the **staging area** (changes you've marked with `add`), and the **repository** (snapshots saved with `commit`).

## Checking status and history

Two commands you'll run constantly: `git status` shows what's changed and what's staged, and `git log` shows the history of commits.

```bash
git status
git log --oneline
```

Every commit needs a clear message. Write it in the present tense, describing what the change does — for example, `Fix off-by-one error in loop`.

## Connecting to GitHub

Create an empty repo on GitHub, then link your local one to it and push. **Push** sends your commits up; **pull** brings new commits down.

```bash
git remote add origin https://github.com/you/project.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
```

## Branches

A **branch** is a separate line of work. You can build a feature on a branch without touching `main`. When it works, you **merge** it back.

```bash
git switch -c add-login
# ...make changes, add, commit...
git switch main
git merge add-login
```

## Ignore the things you should never commit

Create a file called `.gitignore` listing things Git should skip — secrets, your virtual environment, and data files.

```bash
.env
venv/
__pycache__/
*.csv
```

## Your task

Put one of your Python scripts under Git, push it to a new GitHub repo, and add a `.gitignore`.

slides.title: Git & GitHub fundamentals
slides.narration: Welcome back. In this lesson we tackle a skill every professional engineer uses every single day: version control with Git, and sharing your work on GitHub. By the end you'll be able to track changes to your code, save snapshots you can always return to, and push your projects online where the whole world, including future employers, can see them.

slides.title: Why version control?
bullets: No more report_final_v2_REALLY_final.py.
Records snapshots of your work over time.
See what changed, when, and why.
Roll back safely when you break things.
slides.narration: Let's start with the problem version control solves. You've probably saved files as report final, then report final version two, then report final really final. It's chaos. Version control records snapshots of your whole project over time, so you can see exactly what changed, when, and why. And if you break something, you can roll back to a working version with confidence.

slides.title: Git vs GitHub
bullets: Git is the tool that runs on your computer.
GitHub is a website that hosts Git repos.
Git works fine with no internet.
GitHub adds backup and collaboration.
slides.narration: People mix these two up constantly, so let's be precise. Git is the version-control tool that runs locally on your machine. It works perfectly with no internet at all. GitHub is a website that stores copies of your Git repositories in the cloud. Git tracks your changes; GitHub backs them up and lets you collaborate. You can use Git without GitHub, but together they're a powerful pair.

slides.title: Your first repository
bullets: A repo is a folder Git is watching.
git init starts tracking it.
add stages a change; commit saves it.
Each commit needs a message.
slides.code:
git init
git add hello.py
git commit -m "Add hello.py"
slides.narration: A repository, or repo, is simply a folder that Git is watching. You start one with git init. Then the rhythm is: git add to stage the changes you care about, and git commit to save them as a permanent snapshot. Notice the dash m flag — every commit needs a short message describing what you did.

slides.title: The three areas
bullets: Working directory: your actual files.
Staging area: changes marked with add.
Repository: snapshots saved with commit.
add moves to staging, commit moves to history.
slides.narration: It helps to picture three areas. First, your working directory — the real files you edit. Second, the staging area, which holds the changes you've marked with git add. Third, the repository, the permanent history of commits. So git add moves a change into staging, and git commit moves everything staged into the history. Understanding these three areas makes Git click.

slides.title: Status and history
bullets: git status shows what's changed and staged.
git log shows your commit history.
Run status constantly — it's your map.
Write clear, present-tense messages.
slides.narration: Two commands you'll run all the time. Git status tells you what has changed and what is currently staged — think of it as your map, run it often. Git log shows the history of commits you've made; adding dash dash oneline gives a tidy summary. And always write clear commit messages in the present tense, like fix off by one error in loop.

slides.title: Connecting to GitHub
bullets: Create an empty repo on GitHub first.
Link it as a remote called origin.
push sends commits up to GitHub.
pull brings new commits down.
slides.code:
git remote add origin <url>
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
slides.narration: Now let's get your code online. First create an empty repository on GitHub. Then link your local repo to it with git remote add origin, giving it the U R L. The word push means sending your commits up to GitHub, and pull means bringing new commits down. That first push uses dash u to remember the connection, so next time you just type git push.

slides.title: Branches
bullets: A branch is a separate line of work.
Build a feature without touching main.
Merge it back when it works.
Discard it if it doesn't — main stays safe.
slides.code:
git switch -c add-login
# edit, add, commit
git switch main
git merge add-login
slides.narration: Here's where Git really shines: branches. A branch is a separate line of work. You can build a new feature on its own branch without ever touching your main branch. If it works, you merge it back into main. If it doesn't, you just throw the branch away. Either way, your main branch stays clean and working — which matters enormously once you're collaborating.

slides.title: What NOT to commit
bullets: Never commit passwords or .env files.
Skip your virtual environment, venv.
Skip caches and big data files.
List them in a .gitignore file.
slides.narration: One critical safety lesson: some things must never go into Git. Never commit passwords, A P I keys, or your dot env file — leaked secrets are a real and serious problem. Also skip your virtual environment and large data files; they just bloat the repo. You list all of these in a special file called dot gitignore, and Git will quietly leave them alone.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Committing secrets or your venv folder.
Forgetting add before commit.
Vague messages like 'stuff' or 'fix'.
Pushing before you commit.
slides.narration: Let's flag the traps that catch beginners. One: committing secrets or your virtual environment because you forgot a gitignore. Two: forgetting to add before you commit, so nothing actually gets saved. Three: writing useless messages like stuff or fix that tell future-you nothing. And four: trying to push when you haven't committed yet. Avoid these and you'll look like a pro.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Git tracks changes; GitHub hosts them online.
Workflow: add, then commit, then push.
Branches let you work safely off main.
Use .gitignore to keep secrets out.
Task: push a script to a new GitHub repo.
slides.narration: Let's recap. Git is the tool that tracks changes on your machine, and GitHub hosts your repositories online. The core workflow is add, then commit, then push. Branches let you work safely without breaking main, and a dot gitignore keeps secrets and clutter out. Your task before the next lesson: take one of your Python scripts, put it under Git, push it to a brand-new GitHub repo, and add a gitignore. Great work — I'll see you next time.
